title: Doing Yourself Out of a Job
subtitle: The goal of leadership is multiplication, not indispensability, and the leader who cannot let go has mistaken his own grip for faithfulness.

sections.title: The Job Is to Make Yourself Unnecessary
sections.body:
Paul tells Timothy what to do with what he has received. The things you have heard from me, entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also. Count the generations in that one sentence. Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, faithful men to others. Four generations of leaders in a single command, and Paul is in the first one, already planning his own replacement.

That is the aim of all spiritual leadership, and most of us miss it. The job is not to be indispensable. The job is to make yourself unnecessary, to pour your life into people who will carry the thing after you and beyond you and without you. The leader who builds a ministry that collapses when he leaves has not succeeded, he has failed in the most flattering way possible, by making himself so central that the work cannot outlive his presence.

Not a monument. A movement. The monument lasts as long as the man. The movement multiplies past him. And the difference between the two is whether the leader spent his life being the answer or spent it raising up people who could answer without him.

sections.title: Why the Leader Cannot Let Go
sections.body:
We say we want to raise up leaders, and then we cannot let go of anything, and the gap between what we say and what we do has a cause, and the cause is in us.

Being needed feels like being loved. The leader whose whole identity is wrapped in his indispensability cannot release the work, because releasing it means becoming less needed, and becoming less needed feels like dying. So he holds on. He delegates the trivial and keeps the essential. He trains people just enough to assist him and never enough to replace him. He builds dependency and calls it discipleship, and he does not see that he is protecting his own significance at the cost of the kingdom's growth.

I know this because I have done it. I have kept tasks I should have given away, told myself no one else could do them as well, which was sometimes even true, and missed the point entirely. The point was never that someone else would do it as well. The point was that someone else would learn to do it at all, and grow, and eventually surpass me, and the holding on that felt like excellence was actually fear wearing excellence as a disguise. The leader who cannot let go has made himself the ceiling of everything he leads.

sections.title: Delegating So People Actually Grow
sections.body:
Real delegation is not dumping tasks. It is transferring responsibility and authority together, and most leaders transfer the first while keeping the second, which produces frustrated people who are accountable for outcomes they have no power to shape.

Give the whole thing, not the pieces. Hand someone a real responsibility with the authority to make decisions about it, including decisions you would have made differently. The four stages are old and they work. I do it and you watch. I do it and you help. You do it and I help. You do it and I watch. Most leaders stop at the second stage forever, keeping the doing while letting people help, and they call the permanent assistant a leader-in-training who never finishes training.

Let people fail in survivable ways. The mistake you protect them from is the lesson you deny them. If you redo their work, correct every decision, hover over every choice, you are not raising a leader, you are raising a dependent, and the moment you step away the whole thing falls because you never actually let go of any of it. Delegation that costs you nothing has accomplished nothing. It costs you control, and the willingness to pay that price is the difference between a leader who multiplies and a leader who merely accumulates helpers.

sections.title: Succession, and the Refusal to Plan It
sections.body:
Every leader will leave. By death, by transition, by decline, the day comes for all of us, and the only question is whether we prepared for it or pretended it would not happen. The refusal to plan succession is one of the most common and most damaging failures in church leadership, and it is almost always rooted in the same fear of being unnecessary.

Moses, at the end, did not cling. He laid hands on Joshua before the people and transferred the leadership publicly, while he was still standing, so that Israel would know who would lead them when he was gone. He did not make himself the last word. He made himself a link in a chain, and the chain went forward. That is what a faithful leader does. He names and trains and blesses his successors while he still has the strength to do it well.

Start early, long before you must. Identify the people who could lead after you and pour into them deliberately. Give them real responsibility now so they are tested before the day arrives, not handed an untested crown in a crisis. And then, the hardest thing, bless them publicly and step back genuinely, do not hover as a shadow over the one who follows you, second-guessing, undermining, making the transition impossible because you could not actually let go. The leader who will not plan his own succession is telling the truth about his own heart. He would rather the thing die with him than thrive without him.

sections.title: The Seed That Has to Fall
sections.body:
Jesus said unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies, it bears much fruit. He said it about his own death, and it is also the law of every leader who wants to multiply rather than merely persist.

The seed that refuses to fall stays a seed. Impressive, intact, alone. It can sit on the shelf admired and produce nothing, because it would not go into the ground and die. The leader who clings to his indispensability is that seed. He keeps his significance whole and produces no harvest, because the harvest only comes through a death, the death of being needed, the death of being central, the death of being the one without whom nothing happens.

The leader who dies to that bears much fruit. He raises people who surpass him. He builds something that outlives him. He gets to the end and finds the work going forward in hands he trained, and he is glad, genuinely glad, to be no longer necessary, because necessity was never the point. Fruit was the point.

I am still learning to fall. I still like being the seed on the shelf, intact and admired. But the ground is where the harvest is, and a leader who will not go into it will stand alone at the end, holding a significance that dies with him, having multiplied nothing. The grain has to fall. There is no fruit on the shelf.
